1. Will you never, then, my soul, be good and simple, unified and naked, plainer to see than the body that surrounds you? Will you never know what it is to have an affectionate and contented disposition? Will you never be full, lacking nothing, longing for nothing more, wanting nothing, whether living or lifeless, for the sake of enjoying pleasures? Will you never stop wanting more time in which to enjoy them longer, or a place, or a pleasant climate, or people you could live with in harmony? Will you not instead be satisfied with your present condition and pleased with everything around you? Will you not convince yourself that you have everything, and that it comes from the gods; that everything is well with you, and will be well, whatever pleases them and whatever they will give for the preservation of the perfect living being, the universe? That being is good and just and noble. It brings all things into being and holds them together, and it contains and embraces all the things that are broken up so that other things like them can be produced. Will you never be the kind of person who lives in community with gods and human beings in such a way that you never find fault with them at all, and they never condemn you?

2. Observe what your nature requires insofar as you are governed by nature alone, as a plant is. Then do it and accept it, provided that your nature as a living creature will not be made worse by it. Next you must observe what your nature requires insofar as you are a living creature. And you may allow yourself all of this, provided that your nature as a rational being will not be made worse by it. And a rational being is, by that very fact, also a political being, made for community. Follow these rules, then, and do not trouble yourself about anything else.

3. Everything that happens either happens in a way that nature has formed you to bear, or in a way that nature has not formed you to bear. If it happens to you in a way nature has formed you to bear, do not complain; bear it as nature formed you to bear it. But if it happens in a way nature has not formed you to bear, do not complain either; for it will perish once it has consumed you. Remember, however, that nature has formed you to bear everything that your own opinion can make bearable and tolerable, by thinking that it is either in your interest or your duty to do so.
4. If someone is mistaken, correct him kindly and show him his error. But if you cannot, blame yourself, or not even yourself.
5. Whatever happens to you was prepared for you from all eternity. From eternity, the interwoven chain of causes was spinning together the thread of your existence and of everything that befalls it.

6. Whether the universe is a collection of atoms, or nature is a system, let this be settled first: I am a part of the whole, which is governed by nature. Second, I am in some way closely related to the other parts that are of the same kind as myself. If I remember this, then, since I am a part, I shall not be discontented with anything that is assigned to me from the whole. For nothing is harmful to the part if it is to the benefit of the whole. The whole contains nothing that is not to its own benefit. All natures, indeed, have this principle in common; but the nature of the universe has this further principle: it cannot be forced, even by any cause outside itself, to produce anything harmful to itself. So by remembering that I am a part of such a whole, I shall be content with everything that happens. And since I am in some way closely related to the parts that are of the same kind as myself, I shall do nothing that sets me against others. Instead I shall turn toward those who are of the same kind as myself; I shall direct all my efforts to the common good and turn them away from what is contrary to it. Now if things are done in this way, life must flow on happily, just as you can see that a citizen's life is happy when he keeps to a course of action that benefits his fellow citizens and is content with whatever the state assigns to him.

7. The parts of the whole, by which I mean everything that is naturally contained in the universe, must of necessity perish. But understand "perish" in this sense: they must undergo change. Now if this were by nature both an evil and a necessity for the parts, the whole would not continue in good condition, since its parts are subject to change and are made to perish in various ways. For did Nature herself set out to do harm to the things that are parts of herself, to make them liable to harm and bound by necessity to fall into it? Or did such results come about without her knowing? Both suppositions are incredible. But suppose someone even drops the word Nature, as a power that makes things, and speaks of these things simply as natural. Even then it would be ridiculous to say, on the one hand, that the parts of the whole are by their nature subject to change, and on the other hand to be surprised or resentful as if something were happening against nature. This is especially so since things break up into the very things each of them is made of. For either the elements out of which everything was put together are scattered, or there is a change: what is solid turns to earth, and what is airy turns to air. In this way these parts are taken back into the reason that governs the universe, whether the universe is consumed by fire at fixed periods or renewed by everlasting changes. And do not imagine that the solid part and the airy part have belonged to you since your birth. All of this came into you only yesterday or the day before, so to speak, from the food you ate and the air you breathed in. So it is this, what came in, that changes, not what your mother gave birth to. And suppose that what your mother gave birth to binds you very closely to that other part, the one with its own quality of change: even so, this is no objection at all to what has been said.

8. When you have taken on these names, good, modest, truthful, rational, a person of equanimity, a person of greatness of soul, take care that you do not exchange them for others; and if you should lose them, return to them quickly. And remember that "rational" was meant to signify careful, discerning attention to each individual thing, and freedom from carelessness. "Equanimity" means willingly accepting the things that the common nature assigns to you. "Greatness of soul" means lifting the thinking part of you above the pleasant or painful sensations of the flesh, above that poor thing called fame, above death, and above everything of that kind. If, then, you keep hold of these names, without wanting others to call you by them, you will be a different person and will enter a different life. For to go on being what you have been until now, and to be torn to pieces and soiled in such a life, is the mark of someone very stupid and too fond of his life. He is like those half-eaten fighters in the arena with wild beasts who, though covered with wounds and blood, still beg to be kept alive until the next day, when they will be thrown, in the same state, to the same claws and the same bites. So make yourself secure in these few names. If you are able to stay in them, stay there, as if you had been carried off to some Islands of the Blessed. But if you notice that you are falling out of them and are not keeping your hold, go bravely into some corner where you will keep hold of them; or else leave life at once, not in passion, but simply, freely and modestly, having done at least this one good thing in your life: that you left it in this way. To help you remember these names, however, it will help you greatly to remember the gods: that they do not want to be flattered, but want all rational beings to be made like themselves. And remember that what does the work of a fig tree is a fig tree, that what does the work of a dog is a dog, that what does the work of a bee is a bee, and that what does the work of a human being is a human being.

9. Farce, war, panic, sluggishness, slavery: day by day these will wipe out those sacred principles of yours. How many things do you picture to yourself without studying nature, and how many do you let slip? But you ought to look at everything and do everything in such a way that, at one and the same time, your power of dealing with circumstances is perfected, your power of contemplation is exercised, and the confidence that comes from knowing each individual thing is kept up, not shown off, and yet not hidden either. For when will you enjoy simplicity? When will you enjoy seriousness? And when will you enjoy knowing each individual thing: what it is in its substance, what place it has in the universe, how long it is formed to last, what things it is made of, to whom it can belong, and who are able both to give it and to take it away?

10. A spider is proud when it has caught a fly; one man is proud when he has caught a poor hare, another when he has caught a little fish in a net, another when he has caught wild boars, another bears, another Sarmatians. If you examine their judgments, are they not all robbers?

11. Acquire the habit of looking at how all things change into one another. Attend to it constantly, and train yourself in this part of philosophy. For nothing is so well suited to produce greatness of soul. Such a person has stripped off the body. He sees that he must, no one knows how soon, leave the company of human beings and leave everything here; and so he gives himself wholly to acting justly in everything he does, and in everything else that happens he gives himself over to the nature of the universe. As for what anyone will say or think about him, or do against him, he never even thinks about it. He is content with these two things: acting justly in what he is doing now, and being satisfied with what is assigned to him now. He lays aside all distracting and busy pursuits, and wants nothing else than to travel the straight road by way of the law, and, by traveling that straight road, to follow God.

12. What need is there for anxious suspicion, when it is in your power to find out what ought to be done? If you see clearly, go that way contentedly, without turning back. If you do not see clearly, stop and consult the best advisers. And if other things stand against you, go on as far as your powers allow, with careful thought, keeping to what seems just. For it is best to reach this goal; and if you do fail, let your failure be in attempting it. Whoever follows reason in everything is calm and active at the same time, and also cheerful and composed.

13. As soon as you wake from sleep, ask yourself whether it will make any difference to you if someone else does what is just and right. It will make no difference. You have not forgotten, I suppose, what they are like in bed and at table, these people who put on arrogant airs as they hand out praise or blame to others. Nor have you forgotten what they do, what they avoid and what they pursue, and how they steal and how they rob, not with hands and feet, but with the most precious part of themselves. For by that part, when a person chooses, there come into being faithfulness, modesty, truth, law, and a good divine spirit within, which is to say, happiness.

14. To nature, who gives all things and takes them all back, the person who is educated and modest says: "Give what you will; take back what you will." And he says it not proudly, but obediently, and well pleased with her.

15. Little of your life is left. Live as if on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether someone lives there or here, if everywhere he lives in the world as in a state, one political community. Let people see, let them come to know, a true human being who lives in keeping with nature. If they cannot bear him, let them kill him. For that is better than to live as they do.
16. No longer talk at all about what kind of person a good person ought to be; be one.
17. Constantly keep in view the whole of time and the whole of substance, and consider that every individual thing, in substance, is a fig seed, and in time, a single turn of a hand drill.
18. Look at everything that exists, and notice that it is already breaking up and changing, rotting, as it were, or scattering; or notice that everything is formed by nature to die.

19. Consider what people are like when they are eating, sleeping, having sex, relieving themselves, and so on. Then consider what they are like when they are domineering and arrogant, or angry and scolding from their high position. Yet a short time ago they were slaves to how many, and for what things! And consider what condition they will be in a little while from now.
20. Whatever the nature of the universe brings to each thing is for that thing's good. And it is for its good at the very time that nature brings it.

21. "The earth loves the rain," and "the solemn sky loves"; and the universe loves to make whatever is going to be. So I say to the universe: I love as you love. And is this not also what we mean when we say that this or that "loves" to happen, that is, usually happens?

22. Either you go on living here, and you are used to it by now; or you are going away, and that was your own will; or you are dying, and you have done your duty. Besides these, there is nothing. So take heart.

23. Always keep it clear to yourself that this piece of land is like any other, and that everything here is the same as on a mountaintop, or on the seashore, or wherever you choose to be. For you will find just what Plato says: living within the walls of a city as in a shepherd's fold on a mountain.

24. What is my ruling faculty to me now? What kind of thing am I making it now? What am I using it for now? Is it empty of understanding? Is it cut loose and torn away from life in community with others? Is it so melted into and mixed with this poor flesh that it moves along with it?

25. Someone who runs away from his master is a runaway. But the law is a master, and whoever breaks the law is a runaway. And whoever is grieved, or angry, or afraid is dissatisfied because something has happened, or is happening, or will happen, among the things appointed by the one who rules all things; and he is Law, and assigns to each person what is fitting. So whoever is afraid, or grieved, or angry is a runaway.

26. A man deposits seed in a womb and goes away; then another cause takes it over, works on it, and makes a child. What a thing, from such material! Again, the child passes food down its throat; then another cause takes it over and makes perception and movement, and in short, life and strength and other things besides. How many they are, and how strange! Look, then, at the things that are produced in so hidden a way, and see the power at work, just as we see the power that carries things downward and upward: not with our eyes, but no less plainly.

27. Constantly consider how everything, just as it is now, was the same in times past too; and consider that it will be the same again. Set before your eyes whole plays and whole stages of the same pattern, whatever you know from your own experience or from older history: for example, the whole court of Hadrianus, the whole court of Antoninus, and the whole court of Philippus, of Alexander, of Croesus. For all those were plays just like the ones we see now, only with different actors.

28. Picture everyone who is grieved or discontented at anything as being like a pig at the sacrifice, kicking and squealing. Like that pig, too, is the person who lies on his bed and silently laments the bonds that hold us. And consider that only to the rational being is it given to follow willingly what happens; simply to follow is a necessity laid on all.
29. With each thing you do, one at a time, stop and ask yourself whether death is something terrible because it deprives you of this.

30. When someone's fault offends you, turn at once to yourself and consider how you go wrong in a similar way: for example, in thinking that money is a good thing, or pleasure, or a bit of reputation, and so on. For if you attend to this, you will quickly forget your anger, if you also add this thought: that he is under compulsion, for what else could he do? Or, if you are able, take the compulsion away from him.

31. When you have seen Satyron the Socratic, think of either Eutyches or Hymen; when you have seen Euphrates, think of Eutychion or Silvanus; when you have seen Alciphron, think of Tropaeophorus; when you have seen Xenophon, think of Crito or Severus; and when you have looked at yourself, think of any one of the other Caesars. Do the same in the case of everyone. Then let this thought be in your mind: where are those men now? Nowhere, or nobody knows where. For in this way you will keep seeing human things as smoke and nothing at all, especially if you reflect at the same time that what has once changed will never exist again in all the endless span of time. And you: how brief is the span of your existence? Why are you not content to pass through this short time in an orderly way? What material and what opportunity for your own activity are you running away from? For what else are all these things but exercises for reason, once it has looked carefully and searchingly into the nature of the things that happen in life? Keep at it, then, until you have made these things your own, as a strong stomach makes everything its own, as a blazing fire makes flame and light out of whatever is thrown into it.

32. Do not let anyone be able to say truthfully of you that you are not simple or that you are not good. Let anyone who thinks anything of the kind about you be a liar. And this is entirely in your power. For who can stop you from being good and simple? Only decide to live no longer if you are not such a person. For reason does not allow you to live if you are not.

33. What is it, in this material we have to work with, our life, that can be done or said in the way most in keeping with reason? Whatever it is, you have the power to do it or say it; do not make excuses that you are prevented. You will not stop lamenting until your mind is in this condition: that doing what fits the constitution of a human being, in whatever material is set before you and put in your hands, is to you what luxury is to lovers of pleasure. For a person ought to count as enjoyment everything he has the power to do in keeping with his own nature. And he has that power everywhere. A cylinder is not given the power to move everywhere by its own motion; nor is water, nor fire, nor anything else governed by nature or by a soul without reason. For the things that check them and stand in their way are many. But intelligence and reason can make their way through everything that opposes them, in whatever way they are formed by nature and as they choose. Set before your eyes this ease with which reason will be carried through all things, as fire is carried upward, a stone downward, a cylinder down a slope, and look for nothing further. For all other obstacles either affect only the body, which is a dead thing; or else they do not crush us or do any harm of any kind, except through opinion and through reason itself giving way. For if they did, the one who felt it would at once become bad. Now with all other things that have a certain constitution, whatever harm happens to any of them, the thing so affected is made worse by it. But in the same situation a human being becomes better, if one may say so, and more worthy of praise, by making right use of what befalls him. And finally, remember that nothing harms someone who is truly a citizen unless it harms the state; and nothing harms the state unless it harms law, that is, order. And of the things called misfortunes, not one harms law. So what does not harm law harms neither state nor citizen.

34. For someone who has taken true principles deep into himself, even the briefest saying, any commonplace one, is enough to remind him to be free from grief and fear. For example: "Leaves, some the wind scatters on the ground; so is the race of men." Your children, too, are leaves. Leaves too are those who shout as if they deserved to be believed and hand out praise, or on the other hand curse, or blame and sneer in secret. And leaves, in the same way, are those who will receive a person's fame and pass it on to later times. For all such things "come forth in the season of spring," as the poet says; then the wind throws them down; then the forest puts out other leaves in their place. A brief existence is common to all things; and yet you run from everything and chase after everything as if it would last forever. A little while, and you will close your eyes; and soon someone else will mourn the one who saw you to your grave.

35. The healthy eye ought to see everything visible and not say, "I want green things"; for that is the condition of a diseased eye. The healthy sense of hearing and of smell ought to be ready to perceive everything that can be heard and smelled. The healthy stomach ought to be toward all food as a mill is toward everything it is made to grind. And so the healthy mind ought to be ready for everything that happens. But the mind that says, "Let my dear children live," and "Let everyone praise whatever I do," is an eye looking for green things, or teeth looking for soft things.

36. No one is so fortunate that, when he is dying, there will not be some people standing by who are glad of what is about to happen. Suppose he was a good and wise man: will there not be at least someone who says to himself, "At last we can breathe freely, rid of this schoolmaster. It is true that he was harsh to none of us, but I could tell that he silently condemned us"? That is what is said of a good man. But in our own case, how many other reasons are there for which many people want to be rid of us? So consider this when you are dying, and you will leave more contentedly by thinking: "I am going away from a life in which even my companions, for whom I have struggled so hard, prayed so much and cared so much, themselves want me gone, hoping perhaps to gain some small advantage from it." Why, then, should anyone cling to a longer stay here? Yet do not, for this reason, go away less kindly disposed toward them. Keep your own character: stay friendly, well-meaning and gentle. And on the other hand, do not go as though you were being torn away. When someone dies a quiet death, the poor soul slips easily out of the body; your departure from people ought to be like that. For nature joined you to them and made you their companion. But is she now undoing that bond? Very well: I am parted from them as from my kin, not dragged away resisting, but without being forced. For this too is one of the things that are in keeping with nature.
37. Train yourself, as far as possible, whenever anyone does anything, to ask yourself: "What is this person's purpose in doing this?" But begin with yourself, and examine yourself first.

38. Remember that what pulls the strings is the thing hidden within. That is the power of persuasion; that is life; that, if one may say so, is the human being. When you think about yourself, never include the vessel that surrounds you and the instruments attached to it. For they are like an axe, differing only in this: that they grow on the body. Indeed, without the cause that moves them and holds them back, these parts are of no more use than the weaver's shuttle, the writer's pen, or the driver's whip.
